items.stem: The review calls environmentalism "the last great liberal reform movement of the postwar era." Why "the last"?
options: (A) The political tide turned against federal regulation after the 1970s
(B) Ordinary Americans stopped caring about the environment after 1980 ended
(C) The movement failed to achieve any of its stated goals
(D) Liberal reform movements were outlawed in 1980
items.explanation: "Last" refers to the closing of the political window: the backlash against regulation helped elect Reagan, after which the era of expansive liberal federal reform ended.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The backlash and Reagan's victory mark the end of the postwar liberal reform era.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Environmental concern continued; what ended was the liberal reform momentum in Washington.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The movement won the EPA and three major statutes.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No such law existed; the change was political, not legal.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — environmentalism is the last great liberal reform movement of the postwar era; that backlash helped elect Reagan, who arrived promising to shrink the EPA, not grow it

items.stem: Ronald Reagan arrived in Washington promising to shrink the EPA, not grow it. What does that promise show about the politics of the environment by 1980?
options: (A) Reagan was a longtime supporter of the environmental movement
(B) The anti-regulation backlash had become governing policy
(C) The EPA had already been abolished before he arrived
(D) Environmental laws were repealed in the 1980 election
items.explanation: A presidential candidate campaigning against the EPA shows the backlash had moved from protest to power: shrinking regulation was now a governing program.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Promising to shrink the agency is opposition, not support.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The backlash position — regulation threatens jobs and freedom — had become presidential policy.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The EPA still existed; Reagan promised to shrink it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The laws remained on the books; the fight was over enforcement and scope.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — that backlash helped elect Reagan, who arrived promising to shrink the EPA, not grow it

items.stem: Carson documented that DDT was poisoning ecosystems — and readers. Why did the "and readers" part of her finding matter so much?
options: (A) It proved only farmers were ever affected by pesticides
(B) It showed readers were causing the pollution themselves
(C) It made pollution a human-health issue for a wider audience
(D) It limited the book's appeal to professional scientists
items.explanation: A book about birds alone might have stayed a nature book; showing that readers themselves were being poisoned made it everyone's issue.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The point was that exposure reached ordinary readers, not just farm workers.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Carson blamed the chemical industry and complacency, not individual readers.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Human-health stakes converted a nature concern into a mass concern.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The health angle broadened the audience; it did not narrow it.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — Silent Spring (1962) documented how the pesticide DDT was poisoning ecosystems — and readers

items.stem: The great environmental statutes cluster in 1970–73: the EPA and Clean Air Act in 1970, Clean Water in 1972, Endangered Species in 1973. Why did they come in this burst?
options: (A) The president personally ordered Congress to pass the laws on a fixed schedule
(B) Industry lobbyists wrote the laws and pushed them through Congress
(C) The Supreme Court required Congress to act on pollution
(D) Earth Day and visible disasters created pressure Congress could not ignore
items.explanation: Twenty million people on Earth Day plus oil-coated beaches and a burning river gave Congress both the motive and the political cover to legislate quickly.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Congress responded to public pressure; no presidential timetable drove the burst.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Industry generally resisted the new regulations; it did not author them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No court order produced these statutes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mass mobilization plus visible crisis is what concentrates legislative action.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — on April 22, 1970, some 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day, and Congress responded with the decade's great environmental statutes

items.stem: The Love Canal toxic-waste scandal of 1978 involved a Niagara Falls neighborhood built on a chemical dumping ground. What did it demonstrate?
options: (A) Industrial waste could threaten ordinary homes and families
(B) Canals were the main source of American drinking water supplies
(C) The government had solved industrial pollution by 1978
(D) Toxic waste was only ever a problem in rural areas
items.explanation: Love Canal put pollution inside people's houses and schoolyards, making the threat personal in a way distant spills had not.

option_explanations.A: Correct. A residential neighborhood on top of toxic waste made the danger hit home — literally.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The issue was buried chemical waste under homes, not canal water supply.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The scandal showed pollution problems were unresolved.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Love Canal was a suburban neighborhood, not a rural area.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — the Love Canal toxic-waste scandal (1978)

items.stem: The Cuyahoga River catching fire became one of the environmental movement's most cited images. Why was a burning river politically powerful?
options: (A) It proved that rivers were useless for transportation purposes
(B) It was a vivid, undeniable symbol of industrial pollution
(C) It showed that pollution affected only the state of Ohio
(D) It was staged by activists purely for the cameras
items.explanation: A river so polluted it could burn needed no expert explanation; the image carried the movement's whole argument in a single picture.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The point was the pollution, not the river's usefulness.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Vivid symbols move politics because they make abstract harm instantly legible.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The river's power as a symbol was national, not confined to Ohio.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The fires were real consequences of industrial waste, not staged events.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — a string of visible disasters did the rest: the Santa Barbara oil spill (1969), the Cuyahoga River catching fire, and the Love Canal toxic-waste scandal (1978)

items.stem: In 1970 the federal government created the Environmental Protection Agency. What did creating a permanent agency signal?
options: (A) Washington took lasting responsibility for environmental protection
(B) The states were forbidden from passing their own environmental laws
(C) Pollution in the United States had ended for good
(D) The new agency replaced Congress as the lawmaker on pollution
items.explanation: An agency, unlike a single law, is a permanent institutional commitment: Washington would now police pollution as an ongoing federal job.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Creating the EPA made environmental protection a standing federal function.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. States kept their own environmental authority; the EPA added a federal layer.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The agency was created to fight ongoing pollution, not to mark its end.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Agencies enforce laws; Congress still writes them.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — the Environmental Protection Agency (created 1970)

items.stem: The Santa Barbara spill came in 1969, the first Earth Day in 1970, and the major statutes in 1970–73. What does this sequence show about how the movement worked?
options: (A) Congress acted before the public cared at all
(B) The spill caused Earth Day to be cancelled outright
(C) Legislation came first and the disasters followed afterward
(D) Disaster built alarm, then mobilization, then legislation
items.explanation: The order is the movement's method in miniature: visible disaster creates alarm, Earth Day organizes it, and Congress converts it into law.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Congress acted after Earth Day showed mass concern.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Earth Day happened in 1970, a year after the spill.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The sequence runs the other way: disaster, then mobilization, then law.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Each step created the conditions for the next.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — the Santa Barbara oil spill (1969); on April 22, 1970, some 20 million Americans joined the first Earth Day, and Congress responded with the decade's great environmental statutes

items.stem: Postwar Americans had faith in chemical progress; Silent Spring turned that faith into suspicion. What broader 1960s change does this illustrate?
options: (A) Americans stopped using all chemicals in 1962
(B) The chemical industry collapsed in that year
(C) The decade challenged confidence in science
(D) Carson opposed all forms of technology
items.explanation: Doubting chemical progress was part of a wider 1960s pattern: the automatic trust that science and industry knew best came under skeptical review.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Chemical use continued; what changed was uncritical trust.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The industry survived; its reputation for automatic beneficence did not.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The book belongs to the decade's broader questioning of established authority.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Carson criticized specific chemical practices, not technology as such.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — turning postwar faith in chemical progress into suspicion

items.stem: A historian argues the environmental movement succeeded because it copied the civil rights movement exactly. What is the best evaluation of this argument?
options: (A) The historian's claim is fully correct in every detail
(B) The movements shared a toolkit, but "exactly" overstates it
(C) The two movements had nothing in common
(D) Environmentalism came before the civil rights movement began
items.explanation: The review supports the shared-tools parallel but not identity: borrowing a political method is not the same as copying a movement, and the opponents — segregationists versus industry and anti-regulation conservatives — were different.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. "Exactly" claims too much; the parallel the review draws is about tools, not identity.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It accepts the documented parallel while rejecting the overstatement.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review explicitly draws the parallel on tools and on the backlash wall.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The civil rights movement's major victories came in the 1960s, before the environmental statutes of the 1970s.

items.fact_source: u8.md §Added 2026-10-01 The environment, 1962–1980 — it used the same tools as civil rights (moral claims, media events, federal legislation) and hit the same wall
